title: Ceph File System
content:
The Ceph File System interface creates virtual file systems and stores them as a series
of objects within pools. Ceph assigns these objects to placement groups and distributes or places
them pseudo-randomly in OSDs throughout the cluster.

Typically, the Ceph File System uses two pools:

- **Metadata:** The metadata pool stores the data of the Ceph Metadata Server (MDS), which
generally consists of inodes; that is, the file ownership, permissions, creation date and time, last
modified or accessed date and time, parent directory, and so on.
- **Data:** The data pool stores file data. Ceph may store a file as one or more objects,
typically representing smaller chunks of file data such as extents.

Depending upon the application consuming the Ceph File System interface, usually OpenStack
Platform, users may create, modify, and delete files in a Ceph File System. Ceph handles the create,
retrieve, update, and delete operations of each individual object representing the file.

Deleting files destroys the corresponding objects in an unrecoverable manner. However, residual
data artifacts may continue to reside on storage media until overwritten. Data may also remain in
backup archives.
section_path: Ceph File System

title: Ceph File System
content:
Ceph File System (CephFS) is a distributed file system that integrates seamlessly with the Ceph storage architecture. By leveraging the Ceph RADOS (Reliable Autonomic Distributed Object Store), CephFS provides a scalable and robust file system interface, adhering to POSIX standards.

Figure 1 illustrates integration of Ceph within the Ceph cluster.

Figure 1. Ceph cluster integration

CephFS-based file sharing offers the same desirable features as other storage services on the Ceph platform, including scalability, high availability, and operational efficiency. The following are key Ceph components that enable CephFS to achieve these benefits:

Object Storage Daemons (OSDs)
OSDs are responsible for storing the actual file data in CephFS. Files and directories are represented as objects within RADOS, with OSDs managing data storage, retrieval, and replication to ensure durability and availability. 
Ceph Monitors (MONs)
 MONs maintain the cluster map and monitor the health of the Ceph cluster. They track the state of OSDs and other components, ensuring operational stability and fault tolerance. For CephFS, MONs facilitate the mapping of file system operations to the underlying object storage.
Ceph Managers (MGRs)
MGRs handle cluster management, monitoring, and administrative tasks. They provide an interface for managing the Ceph cluster and integrate with external services like OpenStack Manila and Kubernetes CSI for additional functionalities. 
Ceph Metadata Servers (MDSs)
MDSs manage CephFS metadata, including file and directory operations, access control, and namespace organization. They coordinate with OSDs to ensure consistent and efficient metadata operations. 
Scalability
CephFS scales horizontally with the Ceph cluster, allowing for the addition of OSDs, MONs, and MDSs to increase storage capacity and performance, accommodating large data volumes and high client request rates.
Fault tolerance
Inheriting Ceph fault tolerance, CephFS ensures data durability and availability through replication and erasure coding provided by RADOS, even in the event of hardware failures. 
Unified storage platform
 CephFS integrates with other Ceph storage services such as block storage, object storage, offering a unified platform that simplifies management and supports diverse storage needs.
section_path: Ceph File System

title: Use cases for CephFS
content:
CephFS supports a range of use cases, demonstrating its scalability and flexibility to meet various storage needs. These include:
 
NFS and SMB file sharing
Clients and applications can mount and use CephFS based fileshares via the NFS or alternatively through the SMB protocol (currently available in Technology Preview).
Native CephFS clients
Clients can mount CephFS shares directly using the kernel client (kcephfs) or FUSE (ceph-fuse), benefiting from Ceph’s high throughput and low latency.
Kubernetes storage
CephFS can serve as backend storage for Kubernetes via the Container Storage Interface (CSI) driver, facilitating dynamic provisioning and management of volumes for containerized applications.
section_path: Ceph File System > Use cases for CephFS

title: NFS file services
content:
NFS file services enable you to share files across systems in a distributed environment by using the NFS protocol with either Ceph File System (CephFS) or Ceph Object Storage as the backend.

NFS can be used with either Ceph File System (CephFS) or Ceph Object Storage.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 This documentation uses *NFS share* instead of the earlier term *NFS export*. In the Ceph Dashboard, labels and controls may still refer to NFS export.
section_path: NFS file services

title: NFS implementation architecture
content:
You can deploy one or more NFS service gateways.

The NFS gateways provide access to backend storage while presenting a standard NFS interface to client systems.

NFS gateways act as a protocol layer that enables NFS clients to access data stored in CephFS or Ceph Object Storage without requiring native Ceph client software.
section_path: NFS file services > NFS implementation architecture

title: NFS functions
content:
NFS provides the following functions:

- Accepts NFS client connections.
- Maintains NFS protocol state information.
- Processes file system operations.
- Provides access to CephFS shares.
- Provides access to Object Gateway shares.
- Supports highly available NFS deployments.
section_path: NFS file services > NFS functions

title: Supported NFS protocol versions
content:
IBM Storage Ceph supports the following NFS protocol versions through NFS-Ganesha:

- NFSv4.0
- NFSv4.1
- NFSv4.2
- NFSv3
section_path: NFS file services > Supported NFS protocol versions

title: NFSv4 recommendations
content:
IBM Storage Ceph recommends using NFSv4.x for new deployments.

NFSv4 provides:

- Improved security capabilities.
- Stateful protocol operations.
- Better lock management.
- Improved scalability.
- Enhanced high-availability support.
section_path: NFS file services > NFSv4 recommendations

title: NFSv3 considerations
content: Although NFSv3 is supported, it is not recommended for new deployments because it lacks many of the protocol improvements available in NFSv4, including integrated state management and modern high-availability capabilities.
section_path: NFS file services > NFSv3 considerations

title: Use cases for NFS file shares
content:
NFS file services are used in the following scenarios:

- Providing file-storage-as-a-service (FSaaS) for Linux and UNIX clients.
- Supporting legacy applications that require access through a shared NFS file system.
- Providing a standards-based file access protocol across different operating systems.
- Enabling applications to access Ceph storage without requiring native CephFS clients.
- Ingesting data into IBM Storage Ceph environments before processing or archiving.
- Migrating workloads from traditional NAS environments to IBM Storage Ceph.
section_path: NFS file services > Use cases for NFS file shares

title: Benefits of using NFS
content:
NFS file services provide the following advantages:

- Supports a widely adopted industry-standard file access protocol.
- Enables file access from Linux, UNIX, and other operating systems that support NFS.
- Does not require installation or management of native CephFS clients.
- Simplifies integration with applications that already use NFS-based storage.
- Supports highly available deployments by using multiple NFS gateways.
- Enables access to data in IBM Storage Ceph through a widely supported NFS protocol, making it suitable for environments where native CephFS clients or object storage APIs such as S3 are not practical or supported.
section_path: NFS file services > Benefits of using NFS

title: NFS gateway sizing considerations
content:
The capacity of an NFS gateway depends on several factors, including:

- Client concurrency
- Read and write workload characteristics
- Metadata operation rates
- File sizes and access patterns
- Network bandwidth
- CPU and memory resources
- Backend Ceph cluster performance

When planning an NFS deployment:

- Deploy multiple NFS gateways for production environments.
- Size gateways according to expected throughput and client workloads.
- Monitor CPU, memory, network, and storage utilization.
- Validate performance by using representative workload testing.
- Plan sufficient capacity to accommodate workload growth and failover scenarios.
section_path: NFS file services > NFS gateway sizing considerations

title: High availability for NFS services
content:
IBM Storage Ceph supports highly available NFS deployments by running multiple NFS-Ganesha instances behind an ingress service.

A typical high-availability deployment includes:

- Multiple NFS-Ganesha service instances
- HAProxy for load balancing
- Keepalived for virtual IP (VIP) management

This architecture provides a single client access endpoint while distributing requests across available NFS gateways.
section_path: NFS file services > High availability for NFS services

title: NFS failover behavior
content:
NFS maintains protocol state information, including:

- Locks
- Sessions
- Delegations

Traditional NFS failover relies on a grace-period-based recovery process. During the grace period, clients reclaim state information before normal operation resumes.

As a result:

- New requests can be delayed during recovery.
- Applications can experience temporary I/O delays.
- Client state must be recovered before normal operation resumes.

For deployments that use NFS transparent state migration (Technology Preview), client state information can be maintained across participating NFS servers to reduce recovery delays during failover.
section_path: NFS file services > NFS failover behavior

title: Load-balancing considerations
content:
For multi-gateway deployments:

- Use HAProxy as the ingress load-balancing service.
- Configure client affinity when required to maintain NFS session consistency.
- Use a virtual IP (VIP) to provide a single service endpoint.
- Monitor gateway utilization and client distribution.

HAProxy and Keepalived provide a reference architecture for deploying highly available NFS services with multiple gateway instances.
section_path: NFS file services > Load-balancing considerations

title: Limitations and when to consider alternatives
content:
NFS file services introduce an additional protocol layer between customer systems and the storage backend, which requires NFS gateway infrastructure to be deployed and managed. Gateway sizing and configuration can affect overall performance and scalability, and NFS can introduce additional latency compared to direct storage access methods.

Consider an alternative storage access method for the following workloads:
 
- Applications that require the lowest possible latency.
- Database workloads with strict latency and performance requirements.
- Workloads that benefit from direct native CephFS access.
- Large-scale object-storage use cases that are better suited to Ceph Object Gateway and S3 APIs.
- Environments with extremely large file counts and metadata-intensive operations where native CephFS access might be more appropriate.
section_path: NFS file services > Limitations and when to consider alternatives

title: NFS with CephFS
content:
Ceph File System (CephFS) is a distributed file system designed to provide reliable and scalable storage for large-scale deployments. It is part of the IBM Storage Ceph software-defined storage platform and offers features like data replication, fault tolerance, and scalability. When the Ceph NFS service gateway is used with CephFS, it helps enables clients to access CephFS file systems using the NFS protocol.

Ceph NFS service gateway shows how the NFS service integrates with IBM Storage Ceph and CephFS.

Figure 1. Ceph NFS service gateway

CephFS namespaces can be exported over the NFS protocol using the NFS service NFS server with `ceph nfs` commands.

For more information, see Sharing Ceph File System namespaces over the NFS protocol.

For more information about using the Ceph orchestrator with `cephadm` in the backend to deploy the NFS service gateway, see Managing the NFS service gateway using the Ceph orchestrator.
section_path: NFS with CephFS

title: NFS with Ceph Object Storage
content:
The NFS service is deployed with Ceph Object Storage backend using `cephadm`. The configuration for NFS is stored in the `nfs-pool` pool and shares are managed via the Command-Line-interface (CLI) commands and through the Ceph dashboard.

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 NFS with the Ceph Object Storage backend is not a comprehensive NFS service. Its primary purpose is to assist in the seamless migration of legacy applications that use file to object storage with Ceph object storage by ingesting data through NFS file systems. The data is subsequently accessible through the S3 endpoint as an S3 bucket. For a complete NFS solution with features such as high availability and transparent failover, you should use NFS with CephFS backend.

For more information, see:
 
- Deploying NFS service with Ceph Object Storage backend
- Sharing the namespace with NFS service
- Managing NFS shares

Ceph Object Gateway namespaces can be shared over the file-based NFSv4 protocols, alongside traditional HTTP access protocols (S3 and Swift). In particular, the Ceph Object Gateway can now be configured to provide file-based access when embedded in the NFS service NFS server.

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 Only the NFSv4 protocol is supported when using a `cephadm`-based or Rook-based deployment.
section_path: NFS with Ceph Object Storage

title: Namespace conventions
content:
NFS conforms to Amazon Web Services (AWS) hierarchical namespace conventions which map UNIX-style path names onto S3 buckets and objects.

The top-level of the attached namespace consists of S3 buckets, represented as NFS directories. Files and directories, subordinate to buckets, are each represented as objects, following S3 prefix, and delimiter conventions. `/` is the only supported path delimiter.

For example, if an NFS client has mounted a Ceph Object Gateway namespace at `/nfs`, then a file `/nfs/mybucket/www/index.html` in the NFS namespace corresponds to an RGW object `www/index.html` in a bucket/container `mybucket`.

Because the NFS service presents a hierarchical namespace, some object keys might not map directly to the NFS view.

**Important:** **Note:** Important:

When you access object storage buckets through the NFS service, the system presents a hierarchical file system view instead of the native object key namespace.

The `/` character acts as a directory separator in the NFS protocol. Object keys that contain or start with `/` might not appear or behave as expected in an NFS share.

The NFS service can interpret these keys as directory paths instead of individual objects. As a result, some objects might not be visible, might appear as nested directories, or might be inaccessible through the NFS share.

 Avoid creating object keys that start with `/` or depend on `/` in key names when accessing data through NFS shares. Use object storage APIs to access keys that require full namespace fidelity.
section_path: NFS with Ceph Object Storage > Namespace conventions

title: Limitations on supported operations
content:
The Ceph Object Storage NFS interface supports most operations on files and directories, with the following restrictions:

- Links, including symlinks, are not supported.
- NFS ACLs are not supported.
 
- Unix user and group ownership and permissions *are* supported.
- Directories may not be moved/renamed.
 
- Files may be moved between directories.
- Only full, sequential *write* I/O is supported
 
- Write operations are constrained to be uploads.
- Many typical I/O operations, such as editing files in place will fail as they perform non-sequential stores.
- Some file utilities writing sequentially, for example, some versions of GNU tar, may fail due to infrequent non-sequential stores.
- When mounting via NFS, sequential application I/O can generally be constrained to be written sequentially to the NFS server via a synchronous mount option. For example, `-osync` in Linux.
- NFS clients which cannot mount synchronously, for example, MS Windows, will not be able to upload files.
section_path: NFS with Ceph Object Storage > Limitations on supported operations

title: Reference
content:
For more information on NFS with Ceph Object Storage, see the following:

- Creating indexless buckets
- Advantages of colocating Ceph daemons
section_path: NFS with Ceph Object Storage > Reference

title: NFS high availability through HAProxy and multi-active servers
content:
Ceph supports high availability (HA) for Network File System (NFS) services by using HAProxy as a front-end load balancer for multiple-active NFS server instances.

HAProxy uses a virtual IP (VIP) to route client requests to healthy servers. Ceph ensures that each server runs on a separate host, but if no spare host is available, then it accommodates the failed server on one of the existing hosts. If a server fails, Ceph automatically restarts the failed service on a new/existing host using the same server identity. This approach allows connected clients to continue operations without disruption.
section_path: NFS high availability through HAProxy and multi-active servers

title: NFS high availability architecture
content:
IBM Storage Ceph achieves high availability for NFS services by combining HAProxy and Keepalived. HAProxy acts as a front-end load balancer that routes client requests to healthy NFS servers and maintains session persistence for the stateful NFS protocol. Keepalived provides high availability for HAProxy by managing a VIP, continuously monitoring HAProxy instances, and shifting the VIP between hosts when failures occur.

Figure 1. NFS high availability architectural workflow

Ceph implements high availability for NFS services through VIP-based client access, HAProxy load balancing, and Keepalived failover.
 
Client access through VIP
Clients mount NFS shares using a single VIP instead of individual server IPs. Keepalived hosts the VIP and can move it between hosts during failover.
HAProxy load balancing
HAProxy receives client requests on the VIP and forwards them to backend NFS servers based on health checks and load-balancing algorithms.
Keepalived failover
If the active HAProxy instance fails, Keepalived detects the failure and transfers the VIP to a standby host. This ensures continuous service availability without client-side changes.

This architecture ensures uninterrupted client access to NFS shares even during host or service failures.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:

- HAProxy instances synchronize in-memory stick tables across the cluster to preserve client session state during failover.
- As NFS is a stateful protocol, HAProxy needs to maintain state information for every connected NFS client. If an NFS server fails, Ceph attempts to recover the instance on the same host, if available, or on another host labeled for NFS service.
section_path: NFS high availability through HAProxy and multi-active servers > NFS high availability architecture

title: Fault tolerance and placement count
content:
Fault tolerance is the ability of a system to continue operating correctly even when one or more components fail. The NFS high-availability mechanism relies on `cephadm` to start the failed NFS server on (new / existing host) to maintain service continuity.

With no spare host
The number of hosts equals the placement count.
 
For example, if you configure 3 hosts and set the placement count to 3, all hosts are active initially. If one host fails, there is no spare host. In this case `cephadm` starts the failed NFS server on one of the host where another NFS server is running.

With spare hosts
The number of hosts is higher than the placement count.
 
For example, if you configure 5 hosts and set the placement count to 3, three hosts run active NFS servers, and two hosts remain as spares. If one or two active hosts fail, the service can restart on the spare hosts, ensuring fault tolerance.
section_path: NFS high availability through HAProxy and multi-active servers > Fault tolerance and placement count

title: Key features
content:
Key features of NFS high availability include high availability and failover through HAProxy, virtual IP, and access management and security.

High availability and failover through HAProxy 
HAProxy monitors the health of backend NFS servers and reroutes traffic to healthy instances in case of failure. VIP and heartbeat mechanisms enable seamless failover.
VIP 
HAProxy uses a VIP to provide a consistent access point for clients. The VIP dynamically switches between active and standby nodes during failover, requiring no client-side changes. 
Access management and security 
HAProxy supports IP-based access control, authentication, rate limiting, and traffic filtering using Access Control Lists (ACLs) to enhance security.
section_path: NFS high availability through HAProxy and multi-active servers > Key features

title: Use cases for HAProxy with NFS
content:
Use cases for deploying HAProxy with NFS on CephFS include high availability for NFS shares and failover for storage services.

High availability for NFS shares 
HAProxy ensures NFS clients always connect to an available NFS server, preventing service disruptions. 
Failover for storage services 
If a server fails, HAProxy detects the issue and reroutes traffic to a healthy instance. 

For more information, see High availability for NFS services and High availability for NFS services with active-passive servers.
section_path: NFS high availability through HAProxy and multi-active servers > Use cases for HAProxy with NFS

title: SMB file services
content:
You can access CephFS using the SMB protocol through the SMB suite and samba-container images that are managed by Ceph. The SMB manager module provides an interface for deploying and controlling clusters of SMB services and managing SMB shares.

With the SMB module, a cluster acts as a logical management unit that corresponds to one or more managed SMB services. A cluster can implement high-availability mechanisms or operate without them.

CephFS provides two types of management commands for SMB.
 
Imperative commands
Imperative commands provide direct instructions to create, print, or remove SMB clusters and shares. These commands allow users to manage resources through explicit commands.
Declarative commands
Declarative commands enable users to define and apply resource configurations in JSON or YAML format, allowing for consistent management of SMB clusters and shares.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Ceph managed SMB supports only SMB2 and SMB3 versions of the protocol. SMB1 (CIFS) is not supported.

For more information about SMB protocol on CephFS see, SMB cluster and share management.
section_path: SMB file services

title: NFS services planning
content:
Review protocol requirements, availability requirements, gateway placement, share design, and capacity needs before you deploy NFS services.

Proper planning helps ensure that NFS services meet performance, scalability, and availability requirements while simplifying deployment and future growth.
section_path: NFS services planning

title: NFS protocol considerations
content:
IBM Storage Ceph supports both NFSv4 and NFSv3. NFSv4 is recommended for most deployments because it provides improved security, stateful operations, enhanced file locking, and simplified network requirements compared to NFSv3. Use NFSv3 primarily for compatibility with systems that do not support NFSv4.

Most NFS clients automatically negotiate the highest supported protocol version. In environments where both the client and server support NFSv4, the client typically selects NFSv4 unless another version is explicitly configured.

Consider the following when planning protocol usage:

- Use NFSv4 for new deployments whenever possible.
- Use NFSv3 only when required for system compatibility.
- Standardize on a single protocol version when practical.
- Verify client operating system support before deployment.
section_path: NFS services planning > NFS protocol considerations

title: NFS availability considerations
content:
cephadm manages NFS services, and you can deploy them across multiple hosts to provide service resiliency. IBM Storage Ceph supports ingress services with virtual IP (VIP) addresses to provide a highly available access point for NFS clients.

For production deployments, consider the following:

- Deploy NFS gateways on multiple hosts.
- Configure an ingress service with a virtual IP address.
- Avoid single-host deployments when service availability is a requirement.
- Consider host, network, and power-failure domains when you select NFS gateway placement.
section_path: NFS services planning > NFS availability considerations

title: NFS ingress modes
content:
Ingress services provide a single customer access point for one or more NFS gateways. IBM Storage Ceph supports multiple ingress modes to address different deployment requirements:

Standard HAProxy mode
Use when connection distribution across multiple NFS gateways is required. Client connections are balanced across available gateways through a virtual IP address.
HAProxy protocol mode
Use when load balancing is required and preserving the original client IP address is important for auditing, troubleshooting, or access control purposes.
Keepalive-only mode
Use when a virtual IP address is required but load balancing is not necessary. This mode provides a simpler deployment model while maintaining a consistent customer endpoint.
section_path: NFS services planning > NFS ingress modes

title: NFS gateway placement
content:
Gateway placement affects performance, scalability, and service availability. Each host supports one NFS service daemon. Deploy gateways across multiple hosts to achieve additional capacity and resiliency.

Consider the following recommendations:

- Deploy gateways across multiple hosts for high availability.
- Place gateways on hosts with reliable network connectivity.
- Avoid placing all gateways within a single failure domain.
- Ensure sufficient CPU and memory resources are available for expected workloads.
- Plan for future growth when you determine the initial number of gateway hosts.
section_path: NFS services planning > NFS gateway placement

title: NFS share planning
content:
NFS services can export Ceph File System (CephFS) namespaces and Ceph Object Gateway buckets. Before deployment, identify the storage resources that customers need to access and determine how shares will be organized.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 This documentation uses *NFS share* instead of the earlier term *NFS export*. In the Ceph Dashboard, labels and controls may still refer to NFS export.

Consider the following when planning shares:

- Define a consistent naming convention for shares.
- Determine whether shares require read-only or read-write access.
- Identify any access restrictions that must be applied for customer systems.
- Organize shares according to application, department, tenant, or workload requirements.
- Account for future expansion and additional shares.
section_path: NFS services planning > NFS share planning

title: NFS performance and capacity planning
content:
NFS gateway performance depends on workload characteristics, gateway resources, network bandwidth, and backend storage performance. Read-intensive, write-intensive, and metadata-intensive workloads can produce significantly different performance requirements.

Before deployment, consider the following:

- Estimate the expected number of customer systems.
- Estimate throughput and input/output operations per second (IOPS) requirements.
- Evaluate available network capacity between customer systems and NFS gateways.
- Consider future workload growth.
- Test representative workloads before moving into production.

Because workload requirements vary between environments, validate sizing decisions through workload testing rather than relying solely on generic estimates.

For general installation requirements and deployment procedures, see Installation and upgrade requirements.
section_path: NFS services planning > NFS performance and capacity planning

title: MDS Memory Cache Limit
content:
MDS servers keep their metadata in a separate storage pool, named
`cephfs_metadata` and are the users of Ceph OSDs.

For Ceph File Systems, MDS servers support an entire IBM Storage Ceph cluster, not just a single storage device within the
storage cluster. As a result, their memory requirements can be significant. This is the case
particularly if the workload consists of small to medium-size files, where the ratio of metadata to
data is higher.

For example, to set the `mds_cache_memory_limit` to 2000000000 bytes,
run:
```bash
ceph_conf_overrides:
 mds:
 mds_cache_memory_limit=2000000000
```

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 For a large IBM Storage Ceph cluster with a
metadata-intensive workload, do not put an MDS server on the same node as other memory-intensive
services. Doing so gives you the option to allocate more memory to MDS, for example, sizes greater
than 100 GB.

For more information, see Metadata Server
cache size limits.
section_path: MDS Memory Cache Limit

title: NFS service specification parameters
content: NFS service specifications support common service specification parameters and NFS-specific parameters that control networking, monitoring, protocol support, RDMA, TLS encryption, QoS, and high-availability behavior.
section_path: NFS service specification parameters

title: NFS service specification overview
content: For more information about parameters that are shared across service types, see Common service specification parameters.
section_path: NFS service specification parameters > NFS service specification overview

title: Example NFS service specification
content:
The following example shows the NFS-specific parameters that a service specification supports.

```bash
service_type: nfs
service_id: mynfs

placement:
 hosts:
 - host01
 - host02

networks:
 - 1.2.3.4/24

ip_addrs:
 host01: 10.0.0.100
 host02: 10.0.0.101

spec:
 port: 12345

 monitoring_port: 9587

 monitoring_ip_addrs:
 host01: 10.0.0.123
 host02: 10.0.0.124

 monitoring_networks:
 - 192.168.124.0/24

 enable_nfsv3: true
```

This example deploys the NFS service on two hosts, configures custom data and monitoring ports, binds the service to specific IP addresses, and enables NFSv3 support.
section_path: NFS service specification parameters > Example NFS service specification

title: Core service parameters
content:
port
Specifies the TCP port that the NFS service listens on. The default port is `2049`.
ip_addrs
Maps hosts to specific IP addresses for NFS client traffic.
virtual_ip
Specifies a virtual IP address that NFS daemons bind to when used with keepalived-only ingress configurations.
section_path: NFS service specification parameters > Core service parameters

title: Monitoring parameters
content:
monitoring_port
Specifies the port used for NFS monitoring metrics.
monitoring_ip_addrs
Maps hosts to specific monitoring IP addresses.
monitoring_networks
Specifies the networks used to select monitoring IP addresses.
section_path: NFS service specification parameters > Monitoring parameters

title: Protocol parameters
content:
enable_nfsv3
Enables NFSv3 support. By default, only NFSv4 is enabled.
enable_nlm
Enables Network Lock Manager (NLM) support for NFSv3 clients.
idmap_conf
Specifies custom identity mapping configuration settings.
section_path: NFS service specification parameters > Protocol parameters

title: RDMA parameters
content:
enable_rdma
Enables NFS over Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA).
rdma_port
Specifies the RDMA port. If you omit this parameter, the default NFS Ganesha RDMA port applies.

The following example enables NFS over RDMA:

```bash
service_type: nfs
service_id: mynfs

placement:
 count: 1
 hosts:
 - host01

spec:
 port: 2049
 monitoring_port: 9587
 enable_rdma: true
 rdma_port: 20049
```
section_path: NFS service specification parameters > RDMA parameters

title: Colocation parameters
content:
colocation_ports
Specifies custom port assignments for colocated NFS daemons. Each entry must include data_port, monitoring_port, and cluster_qos_port.
data_port
Specifies the data port for an additional colocated daemon.
monitoring_port
Specifies the monitoring port for an additional colocated daemon.
cluster_qos_port
Specifies the port used for cluster-level QoS communications between NFS daemons.
rdma_port
Specifies the RDMA port for an additional colocated daemon when RDMA is enabled.

The following example deploys multiple NFS daemons on the same hosts by using custom ports:

```bash
service_type: nfs
service_id: mynfs

placement:
 count: 4
 hosts:
 - host01
 - host02

spec:
 port: 2049
 monitoring_port: 9587

 colocation_ports:
 - data_port: 3049
 monitoring_port: 9588
 cluster_qos_port: 31312

 - data_port: 3050
 monitoring_port: 9589
 cluster_qos_port: 31313

 - data_port: 3051
 monitoring_port: 9590
 cluster_qos_port: 31314
```
section_path: NFS service specification parameters > Colocation parameters

title: TLS parameters
content:
ssl
Enables Transport Layer Security (TLS) encryption for the NFS service.
certificate_source
Specifies the certificate source. Supported values include `cephadm-signed`, `inline`, and `reference`.
ssl_cert
Specifies the TLS certificate in Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM) format.
ssl_key
Specifies the TLS private key in PEM format.
ssl_ca_cert
Specifies the TLS CA certificate in PEM format.
custom_sans
Specifies additional Subject Alternative Names (SANs) to include in generated certificates.
tls_ktls
Enables kernel TLS (kTLS).
tls_debug
Enables TLS debugging output.
tls_min_version
Specifies the minimum supported TLS version.
tls_ciphers
Specifies the TLS cipher suites that clients can use.

The following example configures TLS encryption by using inline certificates:

```bash
service_type: nfs
service_id: mynfs

placement:
 hosts:
 - host01

spec:
 port: 12345

 ssl: true
 certificate_source: inline

 ssl_cert: |
 -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
 ...
 -----END CERTIFICATE-----

 ssl_key: |
 -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----
 ...
 -----END PRIVATE KEY-----

 ssl_ca_cert: |
 -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
 ...
 -----END CERTIFICATE-----

 tls_ktls: true
 tls_debug: true
 tls_min_version: TLSv1.3
 tls_ciphers: AES-256
```
section_path: NFS service specification parameters > TLS parameters

title: QoS parameters
content:
cluster_qos_port
Specifies the port used for cluster-level QoS communications between NFS daemons.
cluster_qos_config
Specifies cluster-level QoS settings.

The following example configures cluster-level QoS settings:

```bash
service_type: nfs
service_id: mynfs

placement:
 hosts:
 - host01

spec:
 port: 2049

 cluster_qos_port: 31311

 cluster_qos_config:
 qos_type: PerShare
 enable_bw_control: true
 max_export_write_bw: 100MB
 max_export_read_bw: 100MB
```
section_path: NFS service specification parameters > QoS parameters

title: High availability parameters
content:
enable_haproxy_protocol
Enables HAProxy protocol support for high-availability NFS deployments.

When you use HAProxy protocol support, configure the same value for enable_haproxy_protocol on both the NFS service and the associated ingress service.
section_path: NFS service specification parameters > High availability parameters

title: Managing the MDS service using the Ceph Orchestrator
content:
Use the Ceph Orchestrator with `cephadm` in the backend to deploy the MDS
service.

By default, a Ceph File System (CephFS) uses only one active MDS daemon. However, systems with
many clients benefit from multiple active MDS daemons.

When managing the MDS service by using the Ceph Orchestrator, be sure to have:
- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Root-level access to all the nodes.
- Hosts added to the cluster.
- All manager, monitor, and OSD daemons deployed.

title: Deploying the MDS service with the command-line interface
content:
Using the Ceph Orchestrator, you can deploy the Metadata Server (MDS) service by using
the `placement` specification in the command-line interface.

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Hosts added to the cluster.
- All manager, monitor, and OSD daemons deployed.
section_path: Deploying the MDS service with the command-line interface > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
Ceph File System (CephFS) requires one or more MDS.
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Ensure that you have at least two pools,
one for Ceph file system (CephFS) data and one for CephFS metadata.
For more information about
creating Ceph File Systems, see Creating Ceph File Systems.
To deploy the MDS service with the command-line interface, log in to the `cephadm`
shell.
```bash
[root@host01 ~]# cephadm shell
```
Use one of the following options to
deploy MDS daemons using placement specification.
section_path: Deploying the MDS service with the command-line interface > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
Use ceph fs volume to create the MDS daemons.Creating the
MDS daemons creates the CephFS volume and pools associated with the CephFS, and also starts the MDS
service on the
hosts.
```bash
ceph fs volume create FILESYSTEM_NAME --placement="NUMBER_OF_DAEMONS HOST_NAME_1 HOST_NAME_2 HOST_NAME_3"
```

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 By default, replicated pools are created for this command.

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs volume create test --placement="2 host01 host02"
```

title: Creating the pools, CephFS, and then deploying MDS service using placement
content: specification
section_path: Deploying the MDS service with the command-line interface > Creating the pools, CephFS, and then deploying MDS service using placement

title: Procedure
content:
1. Create the pools for CephFS.

```bash
ceph osd pool create DATA_POOL PG_NUM
ceph osd pool create METADATA_POOL PG_NUM
```

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph osd pool create cephfs_data 64
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph osd pool create cephfs_metadata 64
```
2. Create the file system for the data pools and metadata pools.

```bash
ceph fs new FILESYSTEM_NAME METADATA_POOL DATA_POOL
```

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs new test cephfs_metadata cephfs_data
```
3. Deploy MDS service using the ceph orch apply command.

```bash
ceph orch apply mds FILESYSTEM_NAME --placement="NUMBER_OF_DAEMONS HOST_NAME_1 HOST_NAME_2 HOST_NAME_3"
```

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch apply mds test --placement="2 host01 host02"
```

content:

```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch ls
```

example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs ls
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs status
```
3. List the hosts, daemons, and processes.

```bash
ceph orch ps --daemon_type=DAEMON_NAME
```

For
example,

```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch ps --daemon_type=mds
```

content:
Using the Ceph Orchestrator, you can deploy the MDS service using the service
specification.

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Hosts added to the cluster.
- All manager, monitor, and OSD daemons deployed.

title: About this task
content:
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Ensure that you have at least two pools, one for the Ceph File System (CephFS) data and one
for the CephFS metadata.
section_path: Deploying the MDS service using the service specification > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Create the mds.yaml file.

```bash
touch mds.yaml
```
2. Edit the mds.yaml file.

```bash
service_type: mds
service_id: FILESYSTEM_NAME
placement:
 hosts:
 - HOST_NAME_1
 - HOST_NAME_2
 - HOST_NAME_3
```

For example,
```
service_type: mds
service_id: fs_name
placement:
 hosts:
 - host01
 - host02
```
3. Mount the YAML file under a directory in the container.For
example,
```
[root@host01 ~]# cephadm shell --mount mds.yaml:/var/lib/ceph/mds/mds.yaml
```
4. Navigate to the ceph/mds/ directory.For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# cd /var/lib/ceph/mds/
```
5. Log into the `cephadm` shell.

```bash
cephadm shell
```
6. Navigate to the /ceph/mds/ directory.For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# cd /var/lib/ceph/mds/
```
7. Deploy MDS service using service specification.

```bash
ceph orch apply -i FILE_NAME.yaml
```

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 mds]# ceph orch apply -i mds.yaml
```
8. Once the MDS services is deployed and functional, create the CephFS.

```bash
ceph fs new CEPHFS_NAME METADATA_POOL DATA_POOL
```

For
example,
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph fs new test metadata_pool data_pool
```

processes.

title: Managing the NFS service gateway using the Ceph orchestrator
content:
As a storage administrator, you can use the Orchestrator with `cephadm` in the backend to deploy the NFS service gateway. `cephadm` deploys NFS service using a predefined RADOS pool and optional namespace.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 IBM supports CephFS shares only over the NFS v4.0+ protocol.

NFS service is an open source user-space NFS (Network File System) server that allows the sharing of file systems with the NFS protocol.

For information on all the supported Ceph configurations, see IBM Storage Ceph Supported configurations.
section_path: Managing the NFS service gateway using the Ceph orchestrator

title: Prerequisites
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Root-level access to all the nodes.
- Hosts are added to the cluster.
- All manager, monitor, and OSD daemons are deployed.
section_path: Managing the NFS service gateway using the Ceph orchestrator > Prerequisites

title: Creating the NFS service cluster
content: Create an NFS service cluster using the Ceph Orchestrator.
section_path: Creating the NFS service cluster

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Hosts are added to the cluster.
- All manager, monitor and OSD daemons are deployed.
section_path: Creating the NFS service cluster > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
You can create an NFS service cluster using the `mgr/nfs` module of the Ceph Orchestrator. This module deploys the NFS cluster using `cephadm` in the backend.

This creates a common recovery pool for all NFS service daemons, new user based on `clusterid`, and a common NFS service config RADOS object.

For each daemon, a new user and a common configuration is created in the pool. Although all the clusters have different namespaces with respect to the cluster names, they use the same recovery pool.
section_path: Creating the NFS service cluster > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Log into the `cephadm` shell.
For example,
 
```
[root@host01 ~]# cephadm shell
```
2. Enable the `mgr/nfs` module.

```bash
ceph mgr module enable nfs
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph mgr module enable nfs
```
3. Create the cluster.

```bash
ceph nfs cluster create CLUSTER_NAME ["HOST_NAME_1 HOST_NAME_2 HOST_NAME_3"]
```

The CLUSTER_NAME is an arbitrary string and HOST_NAME_1 is an optional string signifying the hosts to deploy NFS service daemons.

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph nfs cluster create nfsservice "host01 host02"
NFS Cluster Created Successful
```

The NFS service cluster, `nfsservice`, is created with one daemon on `host01` and `host02`.
section_path: Creating the NFS service cluster > Procedure

title: What to do next
content:
Verify the NFS service cluster.
 
- List the cluster details.
 
```bash
ceph nfs cluster ls
```
- Show the NFS cluster information.
 
```bash
ceph nfs cluster info CLUSTER_NAME
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph nfs cluster info nfsservice
```

title: Before you begin
content:

title: About this task
content:
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 IBM supports CephFS exports only over the NFS v4.0+ protocol.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Deploying the NFS service gateway with persistent idmap configuration must be done through the service specification file. To get the specification file, use the following command:
 
```bash
ceph orch ls --service-type nfs --export
```

 After exporting the file, follow the procedure in Deploying NFS with idmap settings.

title: Procedure
content:
1. Log into the `cephadm` shell.
For example,
 
```
[root@host01 ~]# cephadm shell
```
2. Create the RADOS pool namespace, and enable the application.
For Ceph Block Device (`rbd`) pools, enable `rbd`.
 
```bash
ceph osd pool create POOL_NAME
ceph osd pool application enable POOL_NAME freeform/rgw/rbd/cephfs/nfs
rbd pool init -p POOL_NAME
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph osd pool create nfs-pool
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph osd pool application enable nfs-pool nfs
[ceph: root@host01 /]# rbd pool init -p nfs-service
```
3. Deploy NFS service gateway using placement specification in the command line interface.

```bash
ceph orch apply nfs SERVICE_ID --placement="NUMBER_OF_DAEMONS HOST_NAME_1 HOST_NAME_2 HOST_NAME_3"
```

The following example deploys an NFS service cluster `nfsservice` with one daemon on `host01` and `host02`.
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch apply nfs foo --placement="2 host01 host02"
```

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.

section_path: Deploying the NFS service gateway using the service specification > Before you begin

title: Procedure
content:
1. Create the `nfs.yaml` file.
For example,
 
```
[root@host01 ~]# touch nfs.yaml
```
2. Edit the nfs.yaml specification file.

```bash
service_type: nfs
service_id: SERVICE_ID
placement:
 hosts:
 - HOST_NAME_1
 - HOST_NAME_2
```

For example,
 
```
service_type: nfs
service_id: foo
placement:
 hosts:
 - host01
 - host02
```

- Optional: Enable the NLM to support locking for NFS protocol v3 support by adding `enable_nlm: true` in the NFS.yaml specification file.
 
```bash
service_type: nfs
service_id: SERVICE_ID
placement:
 hosts:
 - HOST_NAME_1
 - HOST_NAME_2
spec:
 enable_nlm: true
```

 For example,
 
```
service_type: nfs
service_id: foo
placement:
 hosts:
 - host01
 - host02
spec:
 enable_nlm: true
```
3. Mount the YAML file under a directory in the container.

```bash
cephadm shell --mount nfs.yaml:/var/lib/ceph/nfs.yaml
```

For example,
 
```
[root@host01 ~]# cephadm shell --mount nfs.yaml:/var/lib/ceph/nfs.yaml
```
4. Create the RADOS pool, namespace, and enable RBD.

```bash
ceph osd pool create POOL_NAME
ceph osd pool application enable POOL_NAME rbd
rbd pool init -p POOL_NAME
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph osd pool create nfs-pool
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph osd pool application enable nfs-pool rbd
[ceph: root@host01 /]# rbd pool init -p nfs-pool
```
5. Navigate to the directory.
For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# cd /var/lib/ceph/
```
6. Deploy NFS service gateway using service specification.

```bash
ceph orch apply -i FILE_NAME.yaml
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 ceph]# ceph orch apply -i nfs.yaml
```

title: What to do next
content:
- List the service, by using the ceph orch ls command.
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch ls
```
- List the hosts, daemons, and processes.
 
```bash
ceph orch ps --daemon_type=DAEMON_NAME
```

 For example,

```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch ps --daemon_type=nfs
```

title: About this task
content:
idmap.conf settings can be updated manually under /var/lib/ceph/FSID/NFS-Daemon/etc/ganesha/idmap.conf but when the cluster is upgraded, the file contents get deleted.

Use this procedure to keep the NFS `idmap` settings persistent across upgrades.
section_path: Deploying the NFS service gateway using the service specification > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Edit the nfs.yaml specification file.
Add `idmap_conf` information to the specification file.
 
```bash
service_type: nfs
service_id: nfsganesha
placement:
 hosts:
 - example0
 - example1
 - example2
spec:
 idmap_conf:
 general:
 Domain: domain.org
 mapping:
 Nobody-Group: nfsnobody
 Nobody-User: nfsnobody
```
2. Apply the specification file.

```bash
ceph orch apply -i FILE_NAME.yaml
```
3. Redeploy the NFS daemons.

```bash
ceph orch redeploy nfs.nfsganesha
```
