title: High availability for NFS services
content:
High availability for NFS service enables failover and recovery mechanisms that preserve the stateful nature of the NFS protocol and ensure continued access to file shares.

Network File System (NFS) is a stateful protocol. High availability configurations must maintain state information for every connected NFS client and support recovery in case of failures.

If an NFS server fails, the system attempts to recover the instance on the same node (if available) or on another node labeled for NFS service. Once the server restarts, client recovery is initiated using internal state tracking mechanisms.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 I/O operations might be interrupted during server recovery, but clients do not receive I/O errors unless the server cannot restart.
section_path: High availability for NFS services

title: NFS server gateways
content:
You can deploy NFS in two modes: multi-active (HA) and active-passive.
 
Active-passive
A single NFS server runs with ingress but only in Keepalived mode. This mode is suitable for simple or low-availability setups.
Multi-active (HA)
Multiple NFS servers run behind an ingress service for load balancing and failover. Specify a virtual IP address to deploy HAProxy and `keepalived`, which provide a high-availability NFS front end.
section_path: High availability for NFS services > NFS server gateways

title: Multi-active NFS servers
content:
In multi-active configuration, multiple HAProxy/NFS instances are simultaneously active and serve client requests.

- Multiple NFS server instances run simultaneously across different nodes.
- Each server can independently serve client requests.
- Typically, one NFS server instance runs per node to ensure resource isolation and high availability.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:

- Ensure that NFS is configured with a placement count.
- For multi-active deployments, both the NFS service and the ingress service must be configured by using a specification file.
section_path: High availability for NFS services > Multi-active NFS servers

title: Active-passive NFS server
content:
In an active-passive configuration, only one gateway node is active, while another remains in standby and takes over during failure.

- Single active keepalived/NFS instance
- Standby node monitored via Keepalived
- VIP moves automatically to standby during failure
section_path: High availability for NFS services > Active-passive NFS server

title: High availability for NFS services with active-passive servers
content:
Active-passive NFS service provides high availability by using a single active server with a standby server that takes over during failure.

In this deployment model, a virtual IP (VIP) is configured to provide a single access point for clients. The VIP is automatically reassigned to the standby node when the active node becomes unavailable, ensuring uninterrupted client access without requiring remount operations.
section_path: High availability for NFS services with active-passive servers

title: Deployment model
content:
- Only one NFS daemon actively serves client traffic at a time.
- A secondary node remains in standby and takes over during failure.
- A virtual IP (VIP) is used as the client access endpoint.
- The VIP automatically moves to the standby node during failover.
section_path: High availability for NFS services with active-passive servers > Deployment model

title: Failover behavior
content:
- The standby node takes over when the active node becomes unavailable.
- The virtual IP is reassigned to ensure continued client connectivity.
section_path: High availability for NFS services with active-passive servers > Failover behavior

title: Configure active-passive NFS gateway
content: Configure an active-passive NFS deployment by using a virtual IP managed by an ingress service.
section_path: Configure active-passive NFS gateway

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- Ensure that the Ceph cluster is deployed and healthy.
- Ensure that CephFS or Ceph Object Gateway backend storage is configured.
- Identify the hosts for the NFS service and ingress service.
- Ensure that the required ports are available and not in use.
section_path: Configure active-passive NFS gateway > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
In an active-passive NFS deployment:
 
- Only one NFS daemon actively serves client traffic at a time.
- The ingress service (Keepalived) manages a virtual IP (VIP) by using VRRP mode.
- The VIP provides a single endpoint for client access.
section_path: Configure active-passive NFS gateway > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Create an NFS specification file.

```
vi nfs.yaml
```
2. Define the NFS configuration with placement count 1.

```bash
service_type: nfs
service_id: test
service_name: nfs.test
placement:
 count: 1
 hosts:
 - ceph-node-0
 - ceph-node-1
spec:
 port: 2049
 virtual_ip: 192.168.100.112
```
3. Apply the specification.

```bash
ceph orch apply -i <nfs-spec.yaml>
```
4. Create an ingress specification file.
5. Define the ingress configuration with placement count 1 and keepalive_only as true.

```bash
service_type: ingress
service_id: nfs.test
service_name: ingress.nfs.test
placement:
 count: 1
 hosts:
 - ceph-node-0
 - ceph-node-1
spec:
 backend_service: nfs.test
 first_virtual_router_id: 50
 keepalive_only: true
 monitor_port: 9049
 virtual_ip: 192.168.100.112
```
6. Apply the specification.

```bash
ceph orch apply -i <ingress-spec.yaml>
```
section_path: Configure active-passive NFS gateway > Procedure

title: Procedure
content:
1. Log in to a Ceph node.
2. Run the command to configure active-passive gateway.

```bash
ceph nfs cluster create test '1 grim031 grim032' --ingress --virtual_ip 10.64.66.100 --ingress_mode keepalive-only
```
section_path: Configure active-passive NFS gateway > Procedure

title: What to do next
content:
Verify that the services are properly implemented by performing one or both of the following steps.

- View the IP endpoints. IPs for the individual NFS daemons, and the virtual IP for the ingress service.

```bash
ceph orch ls --service_name=nfs.CLUSTER_NAME
ceph orch ls --service_name=ingress.nfs.CLUSTER_NAME
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch ls --service_name=nfs.mycephnfs

NAME PORTS RUNNING REFRESHED AGE PLACEMENT
nfs.mycephnfs ?:12049 2/2 0s ago 20s host02;host03

[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch ls --service_name=ingress.nfs.mycephnfs

NAME PORTS RUNNING REFRESHED AGE PLACEMENT
ingress.nfs.mycephnfs 10.10.128.75:2049,9049 4/4 46s ago 73s count:2
```
section_path: Configure active-passive NFS gateway > What to do next

title: High availability for NFS services with HAProxy and multi-active servers
content:
High availability Proxy (HAProxy) for Network File System (NFS) is a setup where HAProxy acts as a front-end load balancer for NFS server instances. This configuration enables seamless failover and session recovery while preserving the stateful nature of the NFS protocol.

NFS HAProxy is a proxy server that receives requests on a dedicated virtual IP (VIP). This proxy server operates over Transmission Control Protocol (TCP).

When HAProxy fronts NFS services in a Ceph cluster, clients mount the NFS file share using the VIP instead of the physical NFS server IP address. HAProxy receives client requests and forwards them to backend NFS servers based on the configured load balancing algorithm and current server load.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:

- HAProxy support is available only for NFS version 4 (NFSv4).
- Daemon failover is triggered only if the daemon is absent, either due to explicit removal or because the host is unavailable. A daemon that is present but reporting an error/stopped state does not trigger failover.
section_path: High availability for NFS services with HAProxy and multi-active servers

title: Stateful protocol handling and failover
content:
The following points describe how NFS handles stateful protocol operations and failover.

- NFS is a stateful protocol, so HAProxy must maintain state information for every connected NFS client.
- If an NFS server fails, Ceph attempts to recover the instance on the same node (if available) or on another node labeled for NFS service.
- Once the server restarts, HAProxy initiates client recovery using its internal state tracking.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 I/O operations may be interrupted during server recovery, but clients do not receive I/O errors unless the server cannot restart.
section_path: High availability for NFS services with HAProxy and multi-active servers > Stateful protocol handling and failover

title: Health checks and recovery time
content:
The following points describe how HAProxy performs health checks and manages recovery timing.

- The appropriate health_check_interval value depends on the number of nodes in the cluster.
- For a Ceph cluster with up to five nodes, the configuration process typically completes in approximately 2 minutes. For clusters with up to ten nodes, the process may take around 5 minutes.
 
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Configuration time depends on the size and complexity of the Ceph cluster, as well as the system environment and network conditions.
- For smaller clusters, a value of approximately 2 minutes can be sufficient.
 
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Validate this setting by testing NFS daemon failover scenarios before starting client I/O operations to ensure stable behavior.
- If this combined duration is shorter than the NFS daemon startup time, a recovering backend may be prematurely marked as down, leading to unnecessary traffic redistribution, loss of client affinity, and potential client hangs.
section_path: High availability for NFS services with HAProxy and multi-active servers > Health checks and recovery time

title: NFS transparent state migration (Technology Preview)
content:
NFS transparent state migration improves NFS service availability by maintaining client connection state across NFS server instances.

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 Technology Preview features are not supported with IBM production service level agreements (SLAs), might not be functionally complete, and IBM does not recommend using them for production. These features provide early access to upcoming product features, enabling customers to test functionality and provide feedback during the development process.
section_path: NFS transparent state migration (Technology Preview)

title: Overview
content:
Traditional NFS high availability relies on a grace-period-based recovery mechanism. When an NFS server instance fails and is restarted, new client requests are rejected during a grace period, which is typically 90 seconds. During this period, applications can experience delays in I/O operations while client state is recovered.

NFS transparent state migration introduces a new approach that maintains client connection state across NFS server instances. Because connection state is already available on peer NFS servers, a surviving server can continue processing client requests when a failure occurs.

This approach reduces the impact of NFS server failures on client workloads and improves application availability.
section_path: NFS transparent state migration (Technology Preview) > Overview

title: How transparent state migration works
content:
Client connection state is maintained across participating NFS server instances.

1. The cluster detects the server failure.
2. A peer NFS server uses the available client connection state.
3. Client requests are processed by the surviving server.
4. Application I/O continues with minimal interruption.

Because client state is already available on other NFS server instances, failover does not depend on the traditional grace-period recovery process before servicing new client requests.
section_path: NFS transparent state migration (Technology Preview) > How transparent state migration works

title: Benefits of using NFS transparent state migration
content:
- Reduces application disruption during NFS server failover.
- Eliminates delays associated with the traditional 90-second grace period.
- Maintains client connection state across NFS server instances.
- Preserves client lock state during failover.
- Improves availability for applications that depend on NFS storage.
section_path: NFS transparent state migration (Technology Preview) > Benefits of using NFS transparent state migration

title: NFS transparent state migration limitations
content:
The following limitations apply to NFS transparent state migration:

- NFS transparent state migration does not support high-availability (HA) multi-active deployments.
- Dynamic addition of Ceph nodes is not supported when NFS transparent state migration is enabled.
- NFS transparent state migration can be deployed only by using a specification file.
- A minimum three-node cluster is required to enable NFS transparent state migration.
- NFS transparent state migration is supported only on NFSv4 mounts.
- Restarting all cluster nodes simultaneously causes in-memory NFS transparent state migration state information to be lost.
- NFS transparent state migration supports open, lock, and delegation operations.
- NFS transparent state migration does not maintain lock operation records for entries with granted delegations.
section_path: NFS transparent state migration (Technology Preview) > NFS transparent state migration limitations

title: Failover behavior
content:
The Table 1 compares failover behavior between traditional NFS high availability and NFS transparent state migration.

| Traditional failover | Failover with transparent state migration |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Client state is maintained by the active NFS server only. | Client connection state is maintained across NFS server instances. |
| If the NFS server fails, the service must recover before processing client requests. | A peer NFS server can process requests after detecting a server failure. |
| New client requests are delayed during the grace period. | New client requests are not delayed by the traditional grace period. |
| Applications can experience delays in I/O processing during recovery. | Application workloads continue with minimal disruption. |
| Client state, including lock information, must be recovered as part of the failover process. | Client state remains available during failover. |

For more information on enabling NFS TSM and configuring transparent failover support for NFS services, see Configuring and enabling NFS transparent state migration (Technology Preview).
section_path: NFS transparent state migration (Technology Preview) > Failover behavior

title: Configuring and enabling NFS transparent state migration (Technology Preview)
content: Enable NFS transparent state migration to improve failover behavior by maintaining NFS client state information across participating NFS server instances.
section_path: Configuring and enabling NFS transparent state migration (Technology Preview)

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- A minimum of two NFS nodes are deployed.
- NFSv4 clients are in use.
- A dedicated TSM communication port is available.
- Deploy NFS transparent state migration only by using a service specification file.
section_path: Configuring and enabling NFS transparent state migration (Technology Preview) > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 Technology Preview features are not supported with IBM production service level agreements (SLAs), might not be functionally complete, and IBM does not recommend using them for production. These features provide early access to upcoming product features, enabling customers to test functionality and provide feedback during the development process.
section_path: Configuring and enabling NFS transparent state migration (Technology Preview) > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Add the TSM configuration parameters to the NFS service specification file.

For example,

```bash
service_type: nfs
service_id: nfs-cluster

placement:
 count: 3
 hosts:
 - node1
 - node2
 - node3

spec:
 enable_tsm: true
 tsm_port: 36369
 port: 12049
```

The following parameters can be specified in the NFS service specification:

- `enable_tsm` enables NFS transparent state migration.
- `tsm_port` specifies the port used for TSM peer communication.
2. Verify that the NFS daemons are running.

```bash
ceph orch ps --daemon-type nfs
```
3. Verify the NFS cluster configuration.

```bash
ceph nfs cluster info NFS_SERVICE_ID
```
4. Verify that the TSM communication port is active.

```bash
ss -tnp | grep 36369
```
section_path: Configuring and enabling NFS transparent state migration (Technology Preview) > Procedure

title: Results
content: NFS transparent state migration is enabled. NFS client state information is maintained across participating NFS server instances, improving failover behavior during NFS server failures.
section_path: Configuring and enabling NFS transparent state migration (Technology Preview) > Results

title: Configuring high availability for NFS service
content: Configure NFS gateways in IBM Storage Ceph in active-passive mode to provide a highly available NFS service by using ingress services and virtual IP addresses.
section_path: Configuring high availability for NFS service

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 The NFS service and ingress service run on different hosts. For optimal performance and high availability, configure each service on separate hosts.

- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Hosts are added to the cluster, with roles identified: NFS servers or NFS daemons.
- The NFS module is enabled.
section_path: Configuring high availability for NFS service > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
An *ingress service* provides external access to internal services within a Kubernetes cluster. It uses routing rules defined in ingress resources to direct HTTP and HTTPS traffic to the appropriate backend services.

When a cluster is created with --ingress flag, an ingress service is also deployed to provide high-availability for the NFS servers. This applies only to Ceph clusters. A virtual IP is used to provide a known, stable NFS endpoint that all NFS clients can use to mount. Ceph handles the details of redirecting NFS traffic on the virtual IP to the appropriate backend NFS servers and redeploys NFS servers when they fail.
 
**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 When an ingress service is deployed on the NFS cluster, the backend NFS service servers see the HAProxy’s IP address and not the client’s IP address. As a result, if you are restricting client access based on IP address, access restrictions for NFS shares will not work as expected.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:

- If the active NFS server serving a client becomes unavailable, the client's I/O operations are interrupted until a replacement NFS server is available and the NFS cluster resumes operation.
- In NFS deployments, NFS transparent state migration maintains client connection state across NFS server instances. When an NFS server becomes unavailable, another NFS server can continue processing client requests with minimal disruption. For more information, see NFS transparent state migration (Technology Preview)

Deploying an ingress service for an existing service provides:
 
- A stable, virtual IP that can be used to access the NFS server.
- Failover between hosts when the hosts fail.
- Load distribution across multiple NFS server gateways when necessary.
section_path: Configuring high availability for NFS service > About this task

title: Configure multi-active NFS gateway
content: Configure an multi-active NFS deployment by using NFS behind an ingress service (HAProxy and Keepalived).
section_path: Configure multi-active NFS gateway

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- Ensure that the Ceph cluster is deployed and accessible.
- Ensure that CephFS or Ceph Object Gateway backend services are configured.
- Identify the hosts for NFS daemons and ingress services.
- Ensure that all the manager, monitor, and OSD daemons are deployed.
- Ensure that the number of hosts is greater than the placement count for the NFS service.
- Ensure that the NFS module is enabled.
section_path: Configure multi-active NFS gateway > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
In the multi-active architecture:
 
- Multiple NFS daemons serve the same set of shares backed by CephFS or Ceph Object Gateway.
- HAProxy distributes client traffic across these NFS servers.
- Keepalived manages a virtual IP (VIP) to provide a single service endpoint.

To maintain session consistency, it relies on haproxy stick tables to preserve client-to-server affinity. This ensures that a given client continues to communicate with the same NFS instance.

NFS maintains client state, such as locks, sessions, and delegations, on the server.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 If a client is redirected to a different backend:
 
- The new NFS server cannot reclaim or recognize the client’s state.
- This can result in hung I/O, stale locks, or session recovery failures.
section_path: Configure multi-active NFS gateway > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Log in to the `cephadm` shell.

```bash
[root@host01 ~] cephadm shell
```
2. Create an NFS specification file.

```bash
vi nfs.yaml
```
3. Define the NFS service configuration with placement count.

```bash
service_type: nfs
service_id: NFS_SERVICE_ID
placement:
 count: PLACEMENT_COUNT
 hosts:
 - HOST1
 - HOST2
 - HOST3
spec:
 enable_haproxy_protocol: true|false
 port: NFS_PORT 
colocation_ports:
 data_port: DATA_PORT
 monitoring_port: MONITORING_PORT
 cluster_qos_port: CLUSTER_QOS_PORT
```

`service_type`
Specifies the service type. Set this value to `nfs`.
`service_id`
Specifies a unique identifier for the NFS service.
`placement.hosts`
Specifies the hosts on which the NFS daemons run.
spec.colocation_ports
Specifies the ports required by the NFS daemons when multiple daemons are colocated on the same host.
**data_port:** Port used for data traffic
**monitoring_port:** Port used for monitoring
**cluster_qos_port:** Port used for cluster QoS

For example,
 
```
service_type: nfs
service_id: nfs-cluster

placement:
 count: 2
 hosts:
 - node1
 - node2
 - node3
spec:
 enable_haproxy_protocol: true
 port: 12049
colocation_ports:
 data_port: 3049
 monitoring_port: 9588
 cluster_qos_port: 31312
```

**Note:** **Note:** Note:

- The NFS service must be configured with a placement count to maintain client-server affinity.
- You can define the placement count based on deployment requirements.
- Ensure that the number of hosts exceeds the placement count.
4. Apply the specification.

```bash
ceph orch apply -i NFS_SPEC.yaml
```

For example,
 
```
ceph orch apply -i nfs.yaml
```
5. Create an ingress specification file.

```bash
vi ingress.yaml
```
6. Define the ingress configuration:

```bash
service_type: ingress
service_id: INGRESS_SERVICE_ID
placement:
 hosts:
 - HOST1
 - HOST2
spec:
 backend_service: nfs.nfs-cluster
 enable_haproxy_protocol: %true|false;
 first_virtual_router_id: VRRP_ROUTER_ID
 frontend_port: FRONTEND_PORT
 monitor_port: MONITOR_PORT
 virtual_ip: VIRTUAL_IP
 haproxy_peer_communication_port: HAPROXY_PEER_COMMUNICATION_PORT
 health_check_interval: INTERVAL
```

service_type
Specifies the service type. Set this value to `ingress`.
service_id
Specifies a unique identifier for the ingress service.
placement.hosts
Specifies the hosts on which the ingress service (HAProxy and Keepalived) runs.
backend_service
Specifies the NFS service that the ingress service load-balances.
enable_haproxy_protocol
Enables HAProxy PROXY protocol support so that backend NFS daemons can receive the client IP address.
frontend_port
Specifies the port that is exposed to NFS clients. The default value is typically 2049.
monitor_port
Specifies the port used for HAProxy monitoring and statistics.
virtual_ip
Specifies the virtual IP address that is shared across ingress nodes and used by clients to access the service.
haproxy_peer_communication_port
Specifies the port used for HAProxy peer synchronization, including sharing stick-table information between ingress nodes.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 The default value of health_check_interval is set to 30 seconds. However, you should adjust this value based on your cluster size, workload characteristics, and recovery requirements to ensure optimal performance and failover behavior.
section_path: Configure multi-active NFS gateway > Procedure (part 1)

title: Procedure
content:
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Configure the `health_check_interval` value so that the total failure detection time (interval multiplied by three consecutive failures) is greater than the time required for an NFS daemon to start and become ready. If the detection time is too short, a recovering backend might be marked as unavailable, which can cause traffic re
 
- HAProxy stick-table information is not persistent across restarts. Avoid restarting or redeploying the ingress service (HAProxy and Keepalived) after clients begin accessing the service, as this can disrupt client-to-server affinity.
- NFS daemons can run in a colocated configuration to maintain the required number of backend servers. If an NFS daemon stops or enters an error state, it does not fail over automatically. Clients connected to that daemon can experience hung I/O operations. To recover, unmount and remount the affected client.

```
service_type: ingress
service_id: nfs-cluster
placement:
 hosts:
 - node1
 - node2
spec:
 backend_service: nfs.nfs-cluster
 enable_haproxy_protocol: true
 first_virtual_router_id: 50
 frontend_port: 2049
 monitor_port: 9049
 virtual_ip: 1.2.3.4
 haproxy_peer_communication_port: 1024
 health_check_interval: 5s
```
7. Apply the ingress specification.

```bash
ceph orch apply -i ingress-spec.yaml
```

For example,
 
```
ceph orch apply -i ingress.yaml
```
section_path: Configure multi-active NFS gateway > Procedure (part 2)

title: What to do next
content:
Verify that the services are deployed successfully.
 
```bash
ceph orch ls --service_name=nfs.CLUSTER_NAMEceph orch ls --service_name=ingress.nfs.CLUSTER_NAME
```

For example,
 
```
[root@grim061 ~]# ceph orch ls --service_name=nfs.nfs-cluster

NAME PORTS RUNNING REFRESHED AGE PLACEMENT

nfs.nfs-cluster ?:9587,12049,31311 2/2 5m ago 6m grim061;grim062;grim064;count:2

[root@grim061 ~]#

[root@grim061 ~]# ceph orch ls --service_name=ingress.nfs-cluster

NAME PORTS RUNNING REFRESHED AGE PLACEMENT

ingress.nfs-cluster 10.64.66.242:1024,2049,9049 4/4 44s ago 4m grim061;grim062
```
section_path: Configure multi-active NFS gateway > What to do next

title: Placing a host running multi-active NFS daemons into maintenance mode
content: Move NFS daemons from a host to other nodes before placing the host into maintenance mode to prevent service disruption.
section_path: Placing a host running multi-active NFS daemons into maintenance mode

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- The Ceph cluster is deployed and healthy.
- Replacement hosts are available to run NFS daemons.
- You have administrative access to run Ceph orchestrator commands.
section_path: Placing a host running multi-active NFS daemons into maintenance mode > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
In a multi-active NFS deployment, multiple NFS daemons serve client requests. Before placing a host into maintenance mode, you must relocate any running NFS daemons to other hosts.

This ensures continuous availability of the NFS service and prevents client disruption. If a host is placed into maintenance mode without relocating the daemon, clients connected through that node might experience connection hangs or service interruptions.

Choose one of the following approaches based on your NFS placement configuration:
 
- NFS configured with explicit host placement
- NFS configured with placement labels
section_path: Placing a host running multi-active NFS daemons into maintenance mode > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Identify the host that you want to place into maintenance mode.
2. Update the NFS service specification:

- Remove the host from the `placement.hosts` list.
- Add another available host to maintain the required daemon count.

For example,
 
```
placement:
 count: 2
 hosts:
 - ceph-node-1
 - ceph-node-2
```
3. Apply the updated NFS specification:

```bash
ceph orch apply -i nfs.yaml
```
4. Verify the changes:

- Confirm that the NFS daemon is removed from the original host.
- Confirm that a new NFS daemon is deployed on the replacement host.
5. Place the host into maintenance mode:

```bash
ceph orch host maintenance enter <hostname>
```
section_path: Placing a host running multi-active NFS daemons into maintenance mode > Procedure

title: Procedure
content:
1. Identify the host that you want to place into maintenance mode.
2. Add the NFS placement label to another eligible host:

```bash
ceph orch host label add <hostname label>
```
3. Remove the label from the host that will enter maintenance mode:

```bash
ceph orch host label rm <hostname label>
```
4. Wait for the orchestrator to complete the following actions:

- Remove the NFS daemon from the original host
- Deploy a new NFS daemon on the newly labeled host
5. Verify that the required number of NFS daemons are running and healthy.
6. Place the host into maintenance mode:

```bash
ceph orch host maintenance enter <hostname>
```

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Do not place a host running an active NFS daemon into maintenance mode without first relocating the daemon. Otherwise, clients might experience connection hangs or service disruption.
section_path: Placing a host running multi-active NFS daemons into maintenance mode > Procedure

title: Removing HAProxy from an NFS configuration
content:
Learn to remove a HAProxy from an NFS configuration by using the command-line.

To remove a HAProxy from an NFS configuration, follow the steps in the procedure in section Deleting the NFS service cluster.

To troubleshoot error related to HAProxy for NFS, collect the tcpdump from client side during failover. Also collect the NFS debug logs.
section_path: Removing HAProxy from an NFS configuration

title: Updating the NFS service cluster
content: You can update the NFS service cluster by changing the placement of the daemons on the hosts with `cephadm` in the backend.
section_path: Updating the NFS service cluster

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- Hosts added to the cluster.
- All Manager, Monitor, and OSD daemons deployed.
- NFS service cluster by using the `mgr/nfs` module.
section_path: Updating the NFS service cluster > Before you begin

title: Procedure
content:
1. Log into the `cephadm` shell.
For example,
 
```
[root@host01 ~]# cephadm shell
[ceph: root@host01 /]#
```
2. Update the cluster.

```bash
ceph orch apply nfs CLUSTER_NAME ["HOST_NAME_1,HOST_NAME_2,HOST_NAME_3"]
```

The CLUSTER_NAME is an arbitrary string, HOST_NAME_1 is an optional string signifying the hosts to update the deployed NFS service daemons.

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph orch apply nfs nfsservice "host02"
```

This updates the `nfsservice` cluster on `host02`.
section_path: Updating the NFS service cluster > Procedure

title: What to do next
content:
Verify the updated service cluster.

1. List the cluster details.
 
```bash
ceph nfs cluster ls
```

For example,
 
```
[ceph: root@host01 /]# ceph nfs cluster ls
```

title: NFS specific Kerberos setup
content:
You need to create service principals for both NFS server and client. The respective keys
are stored in the keytab files. These principals are required to set up the initial security context
required by GSS_RPCSEC.
section_path: NFS specific Kerberos setup

title: About this task
content:
The service principals have format like `nfs/@REALM`. You can copy the
*/etc/krb5.conf* file from the working system to the Ceph nodes.
section_path: NFS specific Kerberos setup > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Create service principal for that host:

```bash
[root@host ~]# kinit admin/admin

Password for admin/admin@PUNE.IBM.COM: 
[root@host ~]# kadmin
Authenticating as principal admin/admin@PUNE.IBM.COM with password.
Password for admin/admin@PUNE.IBM.COM:
kadmin: addprinc -randkey nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com
No policy specified for nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com@PUNE.IBM.COM; defaulting to no policy
Principal "nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com@PUNE.IBM.COM" created.
```
2. Add the key to the keytab file:

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 During this step, you are already on the NFS server and using `kadmin`
interface. Here, the keytab operations reflect on the keytab of the NFS server.

```bash
kadmin: ktadd nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com

Entry for principal nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com with kvno 2, encryption type aes256-cts-hmac-sha384-192 added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com with kvno 2, encryption type aes128-cts-hmac-sha256-128 added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com with kvno 2, encryption type aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com with kvno 2, encryption type aes128-cts-hmac-sha1-96 added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com with kvno 2, encryption type camellia256-cts-cmac added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com with kvno 2, encryption type camellia128-cts-cmac added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com with kvno 2, encryption type arcfour-hmac added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
kadmin:
```
3. Run step 1 and 2 on all the Ceph nodes where NFS service containers are running and all
the NFS clients.
section_path: NFS specific Kerberos setup > Procedure

title: NFS service container settings
content: Learn how to configure the NFS service settings in the Ceph environment.
section_path: NFS service container settings

title: Procedure
content:
1. Retrieve the existing NFS service container configuration:

```bash
[ceph: root@host /]# ceph orch ls --service-type nfs --export

service_type: nfs
service_id: c_service
service_name: nfs.c_service
placement:
 hosts:
 - host1
 - host2
 - host3
spec:
 port: 2049
```
2. Modify the container configuration to pass on /etc/krb5.conf and
/etc/krb5.keytab files to the container from the host. These files will be
referred by NFS service at runtime to validate incoming service tickets and secure the communication
between NFS service and NFS client (`krb5p`).

```bash
[root@host ~]# cat nfs.yaml

service_type: nfs
service_id: c_service
service_name: nfs.c_service
placement:
 hosts:
 - host1
 - host2
 - host3
spec:
 port: 2049
extra_container_args:
 - "-v"
 - "/etc/krb5.keytab:/etc/krb5.keytab:ro"
 - "-v"
 - "/etc/krb5.conf:/etc/krb5.conf:ro"
```
3. Make the modified nfs.yaml file available inside the cephadm
shell:

```bash
[root@host ~]# cephadm shell --mount nfs.yaml:/var/lib/ceph/nfs.yaml

Inferring fsid ff1c1498-73ec-11ee-af38-fa163e9a17fd
Inferring config /var/lib/ceph/ff1c1498-73ec-11ee-af38-fa163e9a17fd/mon.ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node1-installer/config
Using ceph image with id 'fada497f9c5f' and tag 'ceph-8.0-rhel-9-containers-candidate-73711-20231018030025' created on 2024-10-18 03:03:39 +0000 UTC
registry-proxy.engineering.ibm.com/rh-osbs/rhceph@sha256:e66e5dd79d021f3204a183f5dbe4537d0c0e4b466df3b2cc4d50cc79c0f34d75
```
4. Verification: Validate whether the file has the required changes:

```bash
[ceph: root@host /]# cat /var/lib/ceph/nfs.yaml

service_type: nfs
service_id: c_service
service_name: nfs.c_service
placement:
 hosts:
 - host1
 - host2
 - host3
spec:
 port: 2049
extra_container_args:
 - "-v"
 - "/etc/krb5.keytab:/etc/krb5.keytab:ro"
 - "-v"
 - "/etc/krb5.conf:/etc/krb5.conf:ro"
```
5. Apply the required changes to NFS service container and redeploy the container:

```bash
[ceph: root@host /]# ceph orch apply -i /var/lib/ceph/nfs.yaml

Scheduled nfs.c_service update...
[ceph: root@ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node1-installer /]# ceph orch redeploy nfs.c_ganesha
Scheduled to redeploy nfs.c_service.1.0.ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node1-installer.sxzuts on host 'ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node1-installer'
Scheduled to redeploy nfs.service.2.0.ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node2.psuvki on host 'ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node2'
Scheduled to redeploy nfs.c_service.0.0.ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node3.qizzvk on host 'ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node3'
```
6. Verification: Validate whether the redeployed service has the required changes:

```bash
[ceph: root@host /]# ceph orch ls --service-type nfs --export

service_type: nfs
service_id: c_service
service_name: nfs.c_service
placement:
 hosts:
 - ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node1-installer
 - ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node2
 - ceph-msaini-qp49z7-node3
extra_container_args:
- -v
- /etc/krb5.keytab:/etc/krb5.keytab:ro
- -v
- /etc/krb5.conf:/etc/krb5.conf:ro
spec:
 port: 2049
```
7. Modify the export definition to have `krb5*` (`krb5`,
`krb5i`, `krb5p`) security flavor:

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 You can create such an export after completing the above setup.

```bash
[ceph: root@host /]# ceph nfs export info c_service/exp1

{
 "access_type": "RW",
 "clients": [],
 "cluster_id": "c_service",
 "export_id": 1,
 "fsal": {
 "fs_name": "fs1",
 "name": "CEPH",
 "user_id": "nfs.c_ganesha.1"
 },
 "path": "/volumes/_nogroup/exp1/81f9a67e-ddf1-4b5a-9fe0-d87effc7ca16",
 "protocols": [
 4
 ],
 "pseudo": "/exp1",
 "sectype": [
 "krb5"
 ],
 "security_label": true,
 "squash": "none",
 "transports": [
 "TCP"
 ]
}
```

content: Understand some of the operations that NFS clients can undertake.

title: Procedure
content:
1. Create service principal.

```bash
kadmin: addprinc -randkey nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com@PUNE.IBM.COM
No policy specified for nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com@PUNE.IBM.COM; defaulting to no policy
Principal "nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com@PUNE.IBM.COM" created.
kadmin: ktadd nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com@PUNE.IBM.COM
Entry for principal nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com@PUNE.IBM.COM with kvno 2, encryption type aes256-cts-hmac-sha384-192 added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com@PUNE.IBM.COM with kvno 2, encryption type aes128-cts-hmac-sha256-128 added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com@PUNE.IBM.COM with kvno 2, encryption type aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com@PUNE.IBM.COM with kvno 2, encryption type aes128-cts-hmac-sha1-96 added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com@PUNE.IBM.COM with kvno 2, encryption type camellia256-cts-cmac added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com@PUNE.IBM.COM with kvno 2, encryption type camellia128-cts-cmac added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
Entry for principal nfs/<hostname>.ibm.com@PUNE.IBM.COM with kvno 2, encryption type arcfour-hmac added to keytab [FILE:/etc/krb5.keytab](file:///etc/krb5.keytab).
```
2. Restart `rpc.gssd` service to take effect of the modified/new keytab file.

```bash
# systemctl restart rpc-gssd
```
3. Mount the NFS share.

Syntax

```bash
[root@host ~]# mount -t nfs -o vers=4.1,port=2049 <IP>:/<export_name> >mount_point>
```

Example

```
mount -t nfs -o vers=4.1,port=2049 10.8.128.233:/ganesha /mnt/test/
```
4. Create users.

Once the NFS share is mounted, regular users are used to work with mounted shares. These regular users (generally local users on the system or users from centralised system like LDAP/AD) need to be part of Kerberos setup. Based on the kind of setup, local users need to be created in KDC as well.

title: Managing NFS shares
content:
As a storage administrator, you can manage the NFS shares that use Ceph Object Gateway or CephFS as the backstore on the Ceph Dashboard. You can deploy and configure, edit and delete the NFS service daemons directly from the dashboard.

The dashboard manages NFS service configuration files that are stored in RADOS objects on the Ceph Cluster. NFS service must store part of their configuration in the Ceph cluster.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 This documentation uses *NFS share* instead of the earlier term *NFS export*. In the Ceph Dashboard, labels and controls may still refer to NFS export.
section_path: Managing NFS shares

title: Configuring NFS service daemons
content: You can configure NFS service on the dashboard for Ceph Object Gateway, CephFS, or both, after their configuration.
section_path: Configuring NFS service daemons

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- A running IBM Storage Ceph.
- Ceph Object Gateway, CephFS, or both are installed and configured on the dashboard.
- Ceph Object Gateway login credentials are added to the dashboard.
- A dedicated pool enabled and tagged with custom tag of `nfs`.
- A minimum of `ganesha-manager` level of access.
section_path: Configuring NFS service daemons > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
NFSv3 (version 3) is supported and enabled for clients that do not yet support NFSv4.2 mounts for CephFS file shares.
 
**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Mount a file share with NFSv3 only when NFSv4.2 is not supported on the client or server side. Both NFS protocols can be used.

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 When using object storage with the NFS service, object keys that contain or start with `/` might not appear as expected in NFS shares. To understand how object keys map to the NFS namespace and why this behavior occurs, see NFS with Ceph Object Storage.

For more information, see the following:
 
- Deploying the Ceph Object Gateway using the command line interface.
- Manually adding Ceph Object Gateway login credentials to the dashboard.
- Creating Ceph Object Gateway users.
- User roles and permissions.
- NFS cluster and share management
section_path: Configuring NFS service daemons > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
These steps can be done for either Object Gateway or CephFS. Follow the specifics for the required setup.
1. Create a pool and namespace.

1. From the dashboard navigation, go to Cluster > Pools and click Create.
2. Select either the `rgw` application for Object Gateway or `cephfs` for CephFS.
3. Complete the form and click Create Pool.
2. Create an NFS service gateway.

1. Go to Administration > Services and click Create.
2. In the Create Service form, from the Type drop-down list, select nfs.
3. Set Placement to Hosts.
4. Add two hosts, in the Hosts selector.
5. Enter Count as 2.
6. Complete the form and click Create Service.
section_path: Configuring NFS service daemons > Procedure

title: What to do next
content:
1. From the command-line, as a root user, check if the NFS service is active and running.
 
```bash
systemctl list-units | grep nfs
```

For example,
 
```
[root@host01 ~]# systemctl list-units | grep nfs
```
2. View the NFS services from Administration > Services.

To create an NFS share, see Configuring NFS shares.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 This documentation uses *NFS share* instead of the earlier term *NFS export*. In the Ceph Dashboard, labels and controls may still refer to NFS export.
section_path: Configuring NFS service daemons > What to do next

title: Configuring NFS shares
content: You can create, edit, and delete CephFS and Ceph Object Gateway NFS shares from the Ceph Dashboard. You can also share the CephFS namespaces over the NFS protocol.
section_path: Configuring NFS shares

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:
 
- A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
- Root-level access to the bootstrapped host.
- A minimum of `NFS-manager` level of access on the Ceph dashboard.
- For NFS with Ceph Object Gateway, an existing Ceph Object Gateway bucket. For more information see Managing Ceph Object Gateway buckets.
- For NFS with Ceph File Systems, an existing CephFS volume and subvolume. For more information see Creating CephFS volumes and Creating CephFS subvolume.
- An existing NFS service. For more information, see Configuring NFS service daemons.
section_path: Configuring NFS shares > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
Create an NFS cluster that creates a common recovery pool for all the NFS service daemons, a new user based on the CLUSTER_ID, and a common NFS service config RADOS objects.

NFSv3 (version 3) is supported and enabled for clients that do not yet support NFSv4.2 mounts for CephFS file shares.

Use NFSv4 for clients and servers that support NFSv4.2 or later.

 For information about NFS cluster and share management through the command-line interface, see NFS cluster and share management.
 

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 This documentation uses *NFS share* instead of the earlier term *NFS export*. In the Ceph Dashboard, labels and controls may still refer to NFS export.
section_path: Configuring NFS shares > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. Go to the NFS page.

- To create an Object Gateway NFS share, go to Object > NFS and click Create.
- To create a CephFS NFS share, go to File > NFS and click Create.
 
Alternatively, create the NFS share directly from the Subvolume groups tab on the File Systems page. Select the subvolume group and click Create NFS Export from the action menu.
2. Complete the Create NFS export form and click Create NFS export to save and continue.

1. For CephFS NFS share, select the Subvolume Group and Subvolume.
2. **Optional: **
Clear the NFS Protocol that you do not want to use. 
Both NFSv4 and NFSv3 protocols are selected by default and be used together.
3. As a root user on the client host, create a directory and mount the NFS share.
Syntax:
 
```bash
mkdir -p /mnt/nfs/
mount -t nfs -o port=2049 HOSTNAME:EXPORT_NAME MOUNT_DIRECTORY
```

Example:
 
```bash
[root@ client ~]# mkdir -p /mnt/nfs/
[root@ client ~]# mount -t nfs -o port=2049 host02:/export1 /mnt/nfs/
```

**Important:** **Note:** Important:

Object keys that contain or start with `/` might not appear as expected in an NFS share.

The NFS service interprets `/` as a directory separator. Some objects might be missing, appear as directories, or be inaccessible.

 Avoid using `/` in object key names when accessing data through NFS shares. Use object storage APIs for consistent access.

title: Rate-limiting in NFS
content:
Learn about the rate-limiting or quality of service (QoS) in NFS.

With the rate-limiting or QoS (quality of service) feature in NFS you can control the client’s read/write bandwidth and rate-limiting of the client's input/output operations (IOPS). This function operates at share and client levels, controlling read/write requests and IOPS. QoS ensures that all clients accessing backend storage receives a fair share of resources.

You can enable QoS for a single node NFS server and multiple instances of NFS servers.

The QoS configuration must be stored in the RADOS object and be accessible by any NFS server within the server group. Also, each share must reside on only one NFS server within the group.

The QoS function in NFS supports both bandwidth control and IOPS control.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 The rate-limiting feature is supported only for NFS version 4 and later.
section_path: Rate-limiting in NFS

title: Bandwidth rate-limiting
content:
NFS bandwidth rate limiting allows administrators to control the amount of bandwidth that NFS clients use when accessing or transferring data from an NFS server. This helps prevent excessive network congestion, ensures fair bandwidth distribution, and optimizes network performance for all users and applications.

The following are supported options in bandwidth rate-limiting:

Per share (share) bandwidth control
Use this option to configure the maximum bandwidth that is allowed per share (share). In this case, QoS makes sure that the cumulative bandwidth of all clients accessing this share does not exceed the set bandwidth. For example, if the bandwidth limit for an share is set to 100 Mbps, any client performing any operation on this share is given only 100 Mbps speed.
Per client bandwidth control
Use this option to configure the maximum bandwidth that is allowed per client. In this case, even if the client accesses more than one share, the total bandwidth that is given to the client will not exceed the set limit. For example, if the client bandwidth is set to 100 Mbps, this client can perform operations on any shares with only 100 Mbps speed.
Per share-per client bandwidth control
Use this option to configure both per share maximum bandwidth and per client maximum bandwidth. In this case, the maximum client bandwidth is controlled to the set limit, while the maximum per share bandwidth is also maintained.
 
For example, if the per share bandwidth is set to 200 Mbps and the bandwidth per client is set to 100 Mbps, client A writing to this share will have a speed of 100 Mbps. If client B writes to the same share, client B will have a rate limit of 100 Mbps, as 100 Mbps is already in use by client A.

In bandwidth rate-limiting, you can configure the maximum read and write bandwidth individually. For example, you can set the maximum write bandwidth to 100 Mbps and the read bandwidth to 200 Mbps.
section_path: Rate-limiting in NFS > Bandwidth rate-limiting

title: Input/output operations (IOPS) rate-limiting
content:
IOPS rate-limiting is a feature that controls the number of input/output operations per second that NFS clients can perform on an NFS server. This helps prevent performance degradation, ensures fair resource allocation, and optimizes storage system efficiency.

Read and write operations consist of multiple underlying tasks. For example, a write operation includes four tasks: get file, open file, write file, and put file. If you set the IOPS limit to 20, only 5 IOPS allowed for each of these tasks.

The following are supported options in IOPS rate-limiting are:

Per share operations control
Use this option to configure the maximum number of IOPS allowed per share. In this case, QoS makes sure that the cumulative number of operations that are performed by all clients accessing this share will not exceed the given limit. For example, if the IOPS limit is set to 20, then any client accessing this share can perform only 5 IOPS.
Per client operations control
Use this option to configure the maximum number of operations that are allowed per client. Irrespective of the number of shares that the client is accessing, the total number of operations that are performed by the client will not exceed this limit. For example, if the IOPS limit for a client is set to 20, then this client can perform only 5 IOPS, irrespective of the number of shares it is accessing.
Per share and per client operations control
Use this option to configure the maximum that is allowed per share and maximum that is allowed per client operations. The total number of operations that are performed by the client is controlled to the set limit. Simultaneously, QoS helps ensure the maximum operations per share limit is kept within the limits. For example, if the IOPS limit for share is set to 20 and the client limit is set to 40, then this client can perform only 5 operations on the share as its limit is set to 20. The client can perform the remaining 3 operations on other shares.

For IOPS rate-limiting, all operations that the client performs are counted together as a single unit.
section_path: Rate-limiting in NFS > Input/output operations (IOPS) rate-limiting

title: Managing SMB service, shares, and clusters
content:
Learn about the SMB file system, how to manage the SMB service, shares and clusters by using the IBM Storage Ceph dashboard.

SMB is an open source implementation of the Server message Block (SMB) protocol that provides file and print services between clients across various operating systems.

The Ceph MGR module for SMB provides an interface for deploying and controlling clusters of SMB services and managing SMB shares. In the `SMB manager` module, a cluster is a logical management unit that maps to one or more managed SMB services that itself is a cluster and might or might not use any high-availability mechanisms.

The orchestration is automatically triggered when a cluster is configured for at least one share. The placement field of the cluster resource is passed on to the orchestration layer and is used to determine on what nodes of the Ceph cluster SMB containers can run.

Currently, SMB services can listen on port 445 only. Due to this restriction, only one SMB server, as part of one cluster, can run on a single Ceph node at a time. Ensure that the placement specs on each cluster do not overlap.

The SMB clusters are fully isolated from each other. If you have sufficient resources in your Ceph cluster, you can run multiple independent clusters that can or cannot join the same Active Directory (AD) domains or forests. You cannot share a directory with multiple different clusters that can have different authentication modes or identity-mapping schemes.
section_path: Managing SMB service, shares, and clusters

title: SMB overview dashboard
content:
Learn about the SMB overview dashboard.

The SMB overview dashboard provides a real-time visualization of SMB (Server Message Block) protocol activity and performance across your IBM Storage Ceph cluster. SMB is commonly used for file sharing in networked environments, and this dashboard enables you to monitor key performance indicators such as throughput, latency, session activity, and I/O operations.This dashboard is intended for system administrators, performance engineers, and support personnel responsible for maintaining high availability and performance of SMB services.

The dashboard also provides per-share performance details depending on the selected share or filters. These values appear across multiple graphs rather than in a single panel. Per-share indicators include:
 
Throughput
Data transfer rate per share (kB/s, MB/s, or GB/s). 

IOPS
Number of input/output operations per second per share. 

Latency
 Average response time per share, measured in microseconds (µs).

Ensure that the monitoring stack is installed. For more information, see Deploying the monitoring stack.

Go to the Ceph dashboard > File > SMB > Overview to view the dashboard. You can also access the dashboard from Ceph dashboard > Administration > Services > Grafana > SMB Overview.

To use the dashboard effectively,

- Use the time range selector in the upper-right to adjust the visibility window for metrics.
- Use filters such as Ceph cluster, SMB Cluster, Share , and Client to go into specific nodes or clusters.
- Look for latency and I/O spikes, which can indicate performance degradation or high usage periods.
- Refer to this dashboard during troubleshooting, capacity planning, and performance tuning.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 The Client option is available only as a filter. The dashboard does not display client counts as a separate metric.

The following lists the dashboard pages and descriptions:
 
SMB metrics status
The operational status of the Prometheus exporter collecting SMB metrics. A green `Up` status means that the exporter is running and metrics are actively used.

SMB active sessions
The number of currently active SMB sessions in the cluster.

SMB shares activity
The current activity across all SMB shares within the cluster.

SMB ingress throughput
The rate at which data is received by the SMB server, which is measured in bytes (B). Helps monitor incoming data load from clients.

SMB latency
The average latency for SMB operations, which are measured in microseconds (µs). Useful for identifying performance issues; lower latency values indicate better responsiveness.

SMB egress throughput
The rate at which data is sent out from the SMB server, which is measured in bytes (B).

SMB I/O
The number of SMB input/output operations per second across all nodes. Shows a quick view of overall I/O activity.

SMB I/O per Operation (Graph)
Displays the number of operations per second broken down by SMB operation type (for example: create, read, write, flush, close). This helps identify which SMB operations are generating the most load and how workloads vary over time.

SMB throughput (Graph)
A time series graph plotting ingress and egress throughput across the monitored period. Helps identify usage patterns, peaks, and anomalies over time.

SMB latencies (Graph)
A time series visualization of SMB operation latencies (for example, create, close, flush) for each node.
section_path: SMB overview dashboard

title: About this task
content:
You can opt to create the SMB cluster with 2 different authentication modes:
Standalone
This mode allows you to manually define and manage user accounts and groups within Ceph. It is
suitable for setups where external authentication services are not required. To create an SMB
cluster with Standlone as the authentication mode, see Creating users and groups access resources.
Active Directory (AD) 
This mode integrates with an existing Active Directory domain, enabling centralized
authentication and access control. Users and groups are managed in AD, providing seamless
integration with enterprise environments. To create an SMB cluster with AD as
the authentication mode, see Creating Active Directory access resources.

title: Rate-limiting in SMB
content:
Learn about the rate-limiting or quality of service (QoS) in SMB.

You can configure throughput or Quality of Service (QoS) settings to control performance. QoS settings optimize share performance and improve task execution speed.

You can update QoS limits to apply per-share rate limits on SMB input/output (I/O) operations. These limits include IOPS (Input/Output Operations per Second) and bandwidth (in bytes per second) for both read and write operations.

Supported QoS limits are:
 
- IOPS (Input/Output Operations per Second)
- Bandwidth (bytes per second)
section_path: Rate-limiting in SMB

title: Bandwidth rate-limiting
content:
SMB bandwidth rate limiting controls how much bandwidth SMB clients use when accessing or transferring data from an SMB server. This feature operates at both export and client levels, managing read/write requests and IOPS.

The supported QoS parameters and their valid ranges are listed in Table 1.

| Option | Description | Valid Range |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| read_iops_limit | Maximum number of read operations per second. Set to 0 to disable the limit. | 0 to 1,000,000 |
| write_iops_limit | Maximum number of write operations per second. Set to 0 to disable the limit. | 0 to 1,000,000 |
| read_bw_limit | Maximum bandwidth for read operations. Set to 0 to disable the limit. Specify the value in bytes per second or by using a human-readable string, such as 10M. | 0 to 1 << 40 (≈1 TB/s) |
| write_bw_limit | Maximum bandwidth for write operations. Set to 0 to disable the limit. Specify the value in bytes per second or by using a human-readable string, such as 20M. | 0 to 1 << 40 (≈1 TB/s) |
| read_burst_mult | Burst multiplier for read operations. Allows temporary bursts above the configured limit. For example, a value of 20 applies a burst limit of 2 × the configured rate. | 10 to 100 (1 × to 10 ×), default: 15 (1.5 ×) |
| write_burst_mult | Burst multiplier for write operations. Allows temporary bursts above the configured limit. For example, 20 is 2 times the limit. | 10 to 100 (1 × to 10 ×), default: 15 (1.5 ×) |
| cluster_mode | Controls whether rate limiting is enforced cluster-wide (true) or per node (false) when SMB clustering (CTDB) is enabled. Note: The cluster_mode option is deprecated and is planned for removal in the future. Although the option continues to function currently, it is not recommended to use it in new SMB QoS deployments.this needs to be updated - move it to the description of the optionThis option is deprecated. Although the option continues to function currently, it is not recommended to use it in new SMB QoS deployments. For more information, see Deprecated functionality | true or false, default: true when clustering active |
section_path: Rate-limiting in SMB > Bandwidth rate-limiting

title: Rate-limiting behavior
content:
The following rules define how QoS limits behave when configured for SMB shares:

- All limits are optional.
- Setting a limit to `0` disables that QoS limit.
- Setting all four limits (read and write IOPS and bandwidth) to `0` removes the QoS configuration.
- Burst multipliers apply only when their corresponding limit is enabled (non-zero).
- You can specify bandwidth limits by using human-readable units, such as `10M` or `5G`.
- Specify burst multipliers in tenths. For example, `15` is 1.5 ×, `20` is 2 ×, and `30` is 3 ×.
- The cluster_mode parameter affects behavior only when SMB clustering (CTDB) is enabled.
section_path: Rate-limiting in SMB > Rate-limiting behavior

title: Managing CephFS snapshots
content:
As a storage administrator, you can cretate Ceph File System (CephFS) volume and
subvolume snapshots on the IBM Storage Ceph dashboard.

The Ceph File System (CephFS) snapshots create an immutable, point-in-time view of a Ceph File
System. CephFS snapshots are asynchronous and are kept in a special hidden directory in the CephFS
directory named .snap. You can specify snapshot creation for any directory
within a Ceph File System. When specifying a directory, the snapshot also includes all the
subdirectories beneath it.

CephFS snapshot feature is enabled by default on new Ceph File Systems, but it must be manually
enabled on existing Ceph File Systems.

**Warning:** **Note:** Warning:
 Each Ceph Metadata Server (MDS) cluster allocates the snap identifiers
independently. Using snapshots for multiple Ceph File Systems that are sharing a single pool causes
snapshot collisions, and results in missing file data.
section_path: Managing CephFS snapshots

4. From the Groups and Subvolumes columns, select

per your selection.
- **Subvolume group**: The subvolume group name is already added as per your selection.
Alternatively, you select a different subvolume group from the dropdown list.
- **Subvolume**: The subvolume name is already added as per your selection. Alternatively, you
can select a different subvolume from the dropdown list.

title: CephFS snapshot mirroring
content:
CephFS snapshot mirroring replicates snapshots from a Ceph file system to a file system on a remote cluster, providing data protection for disaster recovery and business continuity.

The Dashboard provides a graphical interface for configuring and managing CephFS snapshot mirroring, reducing the need to perform mirroring operations through the command-line interface (CLI).

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 Creating a mirroring peer relationship establishes connectivity between clusters but does not start data replication. Data replication begins only after mirror paths are configured and snapshots are created for those paths.
section_path: CephFS snapshot mirroring

title: Snapshot mirroring in the Dashboard
content:
The Dashboard enables administrators to:

- Manage mirroring peer relationships.
- Manage mirror paths.
- Manage snapshots for mirrored paths.
- Manage snapshot schedules.
- Manage snapshot checkpoints.
- Monitor mirroring and synchronization status.

For more information about CephFS snapshot mirroring concepts and architecture, see CephFS snapshot mirroring (Technology Preview).
section_path: CephFS snapshot mirroring > Snapshot mirroring in the Dashboard

title: Monitoring snapshot mirroring
content:
The Dashboard provides information about configured mirroring relationships and mirror paths, including:

- Mirroring status
- Synchronization status
- Last synchronization time
- Synchronization duration
- Snapshot checkpoints

This information helps administrators verify that snapshot replication is operating as expected and identify synchronization issues.
section_path: CephFS snapshot mirroring > Monitoring snapshot mirroring

title: Benefits of snapshot mirroring
content:
CephFS snapshot mirroring provides the following benefits:

- Replicates snapshots to a remote cluster for disaster recovery.
- Protects data against site-level failures.
- Maintains replicated snapshots on a secondary cluster.
- Simplifies mirroring management through the Dashboard.
- Provides visibility into synchronization activity and status.
section_path: CephFS snapshot mirroring > Benefits of snapshot mirroring

title: Setting up a CephFS mirroring peer relationship
content: Use the IBM Storage Ceph Dashboard to create a mirroring peer relationship between a source file system and a destination file system.
section_path: Setting up a CephFS mirroring peer relationship

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- The source and destination clusters are reachable over the network.
- You have administrative access to both clusters.
- The source and destination file systems already exist.
section_path: Setting up a CephFS mirroring peer relationship > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
Setting up CephFS snapshot mirroring consists of two phases:

1. Creating a mirroring peer relationship between the source and destination file systems.
2. Configuring mirror paths that define the data to be replicated.

This procedure describes how to create the mirroring peer relationship between the source and destination clusters.

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 Establishing a mirroring peer relationship does not start data replication. After the peer relationship is created, you must configure one or more mirror paths. Snapshots are replicated only for configured mirror paths.
section_path: Setting up a CephFS mirroring peer relationship > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
Preparing the destination cluster
1. In the dashboard, click File > Mirroring.
2. If prompted, enable the CephFS mirroring module.
3. Click Prepare to receive.
4. Select the destination file system.
5. Enter a site name to identify the destination cluster.
6. Specify a CephX user.

- If the user exists, the dashboard updates the permissions that are required for mirroring.
- If the user does not exist, the dashboard creates a new user with the required permissions.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 If you select an existing CephX user, the dashboard automatically updates the user's permissions to support mirroring operations.
7. Click Create token.
8. Copy the generated mirroring token.
Configuring the source cluster
1. In the source cluster dashboard, click File > Mirroring.
2. Click Set up mirroring.
3. Select the source file system.
4. Paste the mirroring token that was generated on the destination cluster.
5. Click Setup Mirroring.
The dashboard creates the mirroring peer relationship. If a `cephfs-mirror` service is not already deployed, the dashboard automatically deploys one.
section_path: Setting up a CephFS mirroring peer relationship > Procedure

title: Results
content: A mirroring peer relationship is created between the source and destination file systems.
section_path: Setting up a CephFS mirroring peer relationship > Results

title: What to do next
content:
After you create the mirroring peer relationship, configure one or more mirror paths to define the directories or subvolumes whose snapshots are replicated to the destination file system. Snapshots are replicated only for configured mirror paths.

For more information, see Configuring CephFS mirror paths.

Optionally, configure snapshot schedule policies for mirrored paths to automate snapshot creation and replication. For more information, see Scheduling CephFS snapshots.
section_path: Setting up a CephFS mirroring peer relationship > What to do next

title: Configuring CephFS mirror paths
content: Configure mirror paths to define the directories or subvolumes whose snapshots Ceph replicates to a destination file system.
section_path: Configuring CephFS mirror paths

title: Before you begin
content:
Before you begin, make sure that you have the following prerequisites in place:

- A Ceph File System (CephFS) mirroring peer relationship exists between the source and destination file systems.
 
For more information, see Setting up a CephFS mirroring peer relationship.
- You have administrative access to the cluster.
section_path: Configuring CephFS mirror paths > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
Mirror paths define the directories or subvolumes that participate in snapshot mirroring. Ceph replicates snapshots only for configured mirror paths.

You can configure multiple mirror paths for a mirroring relationship.

**Important:** **Note:** Important:
 Creating a mirroring peer relationship does not replicate data. Replication begins only after you configure mirror paths and create snapshots for those paths.
section_path: Configuring CephFS mirror paths > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. In the dashboard, click File > Mirroring.
2. Select the mirroring relationship.
3. From the Mirror paths tab, click Add mirror path.
4. Select one or more directories or subvolumes to mirror.
5. Review the configuration and apply the changes.
section_path: Configuring CephFS mirror paths > Procedure

title: Results
content:
The selected directories or subvolumes are now mirror paths.

Ceph can replicate snapshots that you create for the configured mirror paths to the destination file system.
section_path: Configuring CephFS mirror paths > Results

title: What to do next
content:
Optionally, configure snapshot schedule policies for mirror paths to automate snapshot creation and replication.

For more information, see Scheduling CephFS snapshots.
section_path: Configuring CephFS mirror paths > What to do next

title: Viewing and monitoring CephFS snapshot mirroring relationships
content: Use the IBM Storage Ceph dashboard to view configured CephFS snapshot mirroring relationships and monitor their synchronization status.
section_path: Viewing and monitoring CephFS snapshot mirroring relationships

title: Before you begin
content:

| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Mirrored path | The CephFS subvolume or directory configured for mirroring. |
| Target cluster | The remote cluster that receives replicated snapshots. |
| State | The current status of the mirroring relationship. |
| Last synchronization time | The time when the most recent synchronization completed. |
| Synchronization duration | The amount of time required to complete the most recent synchronization. |

title: Scheduling CephFS snapshots
content:
As a storage administrator, you can schedule Ceph File System (CephFS) snapshots on the
IBM Storage Ceph dashboard.

Scheduling Ceph File System (CephFS) snapshots ensures consistent reliable backups at regular
intervals, reducing the risk of data loss. Scheduling snapshots also provides ease of management by
reducing administrative overhead of manually managing backups.

A list of available snapshots for a particular file system, subvolume, or directory is found on
the File > File Systems page.
Use the snapshot list for creating scheduled backups.
section_path: Scheduling CephFS snapshots

title: Creating CephFS snapshot schedule
content:
As a storage administrator, you can create Ceph File System (CephFS) snapshot schedules
on the IBM Storage Ceph dashboard.

title: Before you begin
content: - A running IBM Storage Ceph cluster.
section_path: Creating CephFS snapshot schedule > Before you begin

title: About this task
content:
Create a policy for automatic creation of Ceph File System (CephFS) snapshot of a volume or a
certain directory. You can also define how often you want to schedule it (for example: every hour,
every day, every week, etc.)

You can specify the number of snapshots or a period for which you want to keep the snapshots. All
the older snapshots are deleted when the number of snapshots exceeds or when the retention period is
over
section_path: Creating CephFS snapshot schedule > About this task

title: Procedure
content:
1. From the dashboard navigation, go to
File > File
Systems.File system volumes are listed. Select the file system
where you want to create the snapshot schedule.
2. Go to Snapshot schedules tab.

**Note:** **Note:** Note:
 The Enable is available only if the *snapshot_scheduler *is
disabled on the cluster.

1. **Optional: **Click Enable to enable the
`snapshot_scheduler` module.After enabling the scheduler, wait for the
dashboard to reload and navigate back to the Snapshot schedule
page.
2. Click Create.The Create Snapshot
schedule form opens.
3. Enter the directory name, start date, start time, and schedule.

- Directory: You can search by typing in the path of the directory or
subvolume and select the directory from the suggested list where you want to create the snapshot
schedule.
- Start date: Enter date on which you want the scheduler to start creating
the snapshots. By default the current date is selected.
- Start time: Enter the time at which you want the scheduler to start
creating the snapshots. By default the current time is added.
- Schedule: Enter the number of snapshots and the frequency at which you
want to create the snapshots. Frequency can be hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, yearly or lastest
snapshots.

1. **Optional: **Click Add retention policy if you want to
add retention policy to the schedule. You can add multiple retention policies. Enter the
number of snapshots and the frequency at which you want to retain the snapshots. Frequency can be
hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, yearly or lastest snapshots.
2. Click Create snapshot schedule.A notification is
displayed that the snapshot schedule is created successfully.
